node.label: Haunani-Kay Trask
node.date_label: Review of Linnekin 1986 · “Natives and Anthropologists” 1991 · From a Native Daughter 1993, revised 1999
node.description: A scholar of Hawaiian sovereignty whose 1991 reply to Roger Keesing is a founding exchange over who may interpret the Native past. Keesing had argued that Pacific nationalists idealise and 'invent' their pasts. Trask answered with 'solid evidence from Native forms of history-genealogy', charged that Keesing, 'with many Western academics', assumed that 'Natives don't know very much', and insisted 'We do not need, nor do we want to be "liberated" from our past'. She named Lilikalā Kameʻeleihiwa among the Native historians Keesing had not read. Keesing replied that her 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy was 'a great leap backward'; Linnekin, that 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious'. Kauanui (2016) credits her essay on 'settlers of color' in Hawaiʻi as an earlier settler-colonial analysis.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Haunani-Kay Trask (1949–2021); review of Linnekin, Children of the Land (Hawaiian Journal of History, 1986); 'Natives and Anthropologists: The Colonial Struggle' (1991); From a Native Daughter: Colonialism and Sovereignty in Hawaiʻi (1993; revised 1999); 'Settlers of Color and "Immigrant" Hegemony' (Amerasia, 2000).
node.scope_note: Read in full: 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991) and Keesing's reply; Linnekin's reply in part. From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999) is known through the publisher's description; the 1987 essay of that title and the 2000 essay are unread. No Canadian History PhD in the citation graph cites her (release 2026-10-23); the entry rests on the named, two-sided critique.

proposed_edges.relationship: Answers Keesing's charge that Pacific nationalists 'invent' their pasts with genealogy as 'Native forms of history', against an academic assumption that 'Natives don't know very much'; Keesing and Linnekin replied in the same issue (1991)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991, read in full), pp. 159–161, 164 and 166 n. 4. Replies read: Keesing, the 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy 'a great leap backward' and 'Does she really have to suspend her critical judgment with regard to the past?' (pp. 168–169); Linnekin, 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious' and Trask's view of tradition 'strikingly similar to my own' (pp. 173–174). Neither Keesing nor Linnekin has a node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)
